Volume 15 · Chapter 11

Urban economics, housing and inequality

Advanced Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v15-c10

By the endAnalyze spatial decisions and distribution with equilibrium feedback.

Capability and prerequisites

Analyze location, housing and distribution with equilibrium feedback. Prerequisite: health, education and demographic economics; also use consumer choice, competitive supply, causal inference and the labor chapter's distinction between mobility and selection. Every numerical city, household and experiment here is synthetic. Rents are payments per period; housing asset prices are present values of future net payments and must not be substituted for them.

Who gains when a place becomes more desirable?

A transport improvement shortens a commute. A productive employer expands. A park makes a neighborhood pleasant. People may gain directly, but they also bid for space. Some gains can appear as higher rents, new construction or migration; incumbents, newcomers, owners and renters need not share them equally. A rise in average neighborhood income can result from richer people moving in even if nobody's own income rises. These feedbacks are part of the question, not an afterthought.

Distinguish a place from a population. “Residents after the project” can be a different set of people from “people resident before it.” Specify whether the target includes movers, commuters, owners living elsewhere and future cohorts. A national resource gain is a different object from the municipal tax base or an incumbent renter's welfare. A housing policy also operates at a horizon: a fixed stock this month need not be fixed over a decade, but long-run construction is not instant or costless.

We develop five mechanisms: access creates a rent gradient; housing supply mediates migration; heterogeneous values produce sorting and partially identified rent premiums; inequality measures change with aggregation; and randomized mobility offers identify a particular population and treatment. The models make their closures visible so that a result cannot move silently from one mechanism to another.

1. Location rents compensate for access costs

A household chooses an available dwelling and numeraire consumption. With a fixed housing unit, a common wage w, local amenity a(x), rent r(x) and real commuting cost tx, utility is w−r(x)−tx+a(x). If identical mobile households occupy two locations, their utilities must match: otherwise someone would prefer the better bundle. This gives a bid-rent schedule conditional on the common utility level. It does not mean workers must have equal gross incomes in more general models with different skills, preferences or constraints.

Wheaton’s urban-land lecture introduces commuting compensation and the role of alternative land uses. Our example uses a one-sided line with density one, rather than a radial city; changing geometry changes the relation between population and radius. Housing space, construction and commuting are intentionally simplified. A rent gradient estimated from real addresses would also reflect dwelling quality, employment centers, amenities and sorting, so distance alone is not a causal measure of transport cost.

Worked case 1 — cheaper commuting under two population closures

A closed city has N=4 identical workers on a line x∈[0,4], one dwelling per unit of distance. Each produces w=20 numeraire at the center. Commuting consumes tx real goods, with t=2. Dwellings are costless apart from their land, which could earn r_A=1 per unit in agriculture. Competitive land conversion puts the boundary rent at1. All workers rent from separate owners; profits or land rents are not rebated to them. The primitives are (N,w,t,rA)=(4,20,2,1).

Equal utility and the boundary condition imply r(x)=r_A+t(N−x)=9−2x and u=w−r_A−tN=11. Every occupied location then yields11; land farther out cannot attract workers while covering its alternative return. Total commuting is∫₀⁴2x dx=16, total rent is∫₀⁴(9−2x)dx=20, and worker numeraire consumption is44. Thus (utility,total commute,total rent,worker consumption,differential rent)=(11,16,20,44,16). Workers plus owners receive64after commuting; subtracting the forgone agricultural output4 gives a net resource measure60relative to the same land remaining agricultural.

Now reduce t to1 at no implementation cost for this comparison. Population and boundary stay4. Rent becomes5−x, utility15, commuting8and total rent12. Workers gain16 in aggregate; owners lose8; their combined gain8 equals the real commuting saving. The net resource measure becomes68. The check is (utility,commute,rent,worker gain,owner gain,resource gain)=(15,8,12,16,-8,8). Property owners need not gain from a transport improvement in a closed city with an unchanged boundary.

For a different closure, hold outside worker utility at11 and allow costless entry from a large reservoir while w stays20. Boundary R solves20−1−tR=11, hence R=N=8/t. Reducing t from2to1 expands the city from4to8; worker utility remains11. Differential rent above agriculture is tR²/2, increasing from16to32. The additional land and workers must now be accounted for when calculating national welfare. The unchanged entrant utility and larger rent base describe incidence in this open-city model; the earlier closed-city aggregate gain8 cannot simply be reused.

2. Housing supply and migration jointly determine an equilibrium

Housing supply is a real-resource relation. A developer paying for labor and materials responds to rent, costs, land availability and restrictions. Scarcity payments to an owner are transfers, while construction inputs consume resources. An asset-price rise can include expected future scarcity rents; adding that capitalization to every future rent gain would count the same claim twice. His housing lecture provides context for property attributes and development costs; the market below is an original competitive supply example.

Let ten identical workers freely choose between two cities, with one housing service per worker and no commuting or moving cost. City A pays wage20, city B wage16, each equal to constant marginal numeraire production. Competitive housing supply has aggregate cost Cᵢ(nᵢ)=2nᵢ+nᵢ²/2 and inverse supply rᵢ=2+nᵢ when unconstrained. Think of a continuum of independently owned sites with increasing real service costs. The inframarginal surplus accrues to separate site owners, who consume numeraire and do not enter workers' location utilities. Workers' consumption is wage minus rent; all stated rents leave it positive.

Worked case 2 — a supply cap changes both rents and the population

Let n=n_A, so n_B=10−n. Worker utilities are18−n in A and4+n in B. The unique intersection is n=7, giving common utility11, rents(9,5), and housing costs(77/2,21/2). Both cities must be occupied: at n=0, A is preferable, and at n=10, B is preferable. The utility difference14−2n is strictly decreasing, proving the unique location equilibrium. Primitive and result records are (N,wA,wB,costintercept,costslope)=(10,20,16,2,1) and (nA,nB,rA,rB,u,output,housingcost,total surplus)=(7,3,9,5,11,188,49,139). Worker consumption110 plus owner surplus29 equals139.

Now impose an A housing-service cap of6, allocating the six operating rights to the same site owners. B must accommodate4, so r_B=6 and utility10. For workers to occupy A without excess demand at the market-clearing rent, r_A=20−10=10. A's marginal real cost at6 is8; the extra2is scarcity value from the cap. A housing costs30, receipts60and owner surplus30; B costs16, receipts24and owner surplus8. Thus (nA,nB,rA,rB,u,owner surplus,total surplus)=(6,4,10,6,10,38,138). Workers lose10 in aggregate while owners gain9; the remaining loss1 is real inefficiency under these primitives. Transfers can be much larger than the net resource loss.

For any allocation n∈[0,10], total numeraire net of housing is20n+16(10−n)−C_A(n)−C_B(10−n)=139−(n−7)². This global certificate proves the unconstrained optimum7 and the capped optimum6. Relaxing a cap k from6toward7 raises surplus at marginal rate2(7−k), which initially equals2. There is no pollution, crowding or infrastructure cost omitted inside this model; those are absent assumptions, not evidence that real development has none. A regulation addressing such an externality needs those benefits in the objective before it can be evaluated.

If instead the uncapped A wage becomes22 through an exogenous real productivity increase, n_A=8,n_B=2, rents(10,4), common utility12, output208and housing costs54. Total surplus154 rises by15: workers gain10, owners gain5. A higher nominal wage attracts labor and raises local rent, but its incidence also reaches the other city through outmigration and cheaper housing. Holding the A population and both rents fixed would miss that response.

3. Amenities, sorting and what a rent premium identifies

People value places differently. A household may pay more for school access, quiet, proximity to relatives or a particular commute. Housing prices reflect the marginal choices of households able and willing to compete for available homes. A hedonic price slope is therefore an equilibrium object. Recovering a population's willingness to pay from it requires preferences, budgets, supply and sorting assumptions, not just an attractive regression fit.

Observed spatial separation need not reveal its cause. Price competition, borrowing constraints, discrimination, search frictions and historical exclusion can generate similar residence patterns. The simple preference example below does not prove that actual segregation is chosen freely, efficient or ethically acceptable. It isolates one possible sorting mechanism while leaving those other mechanisms for evidence.

Worked case 3 — a unique allocation can have a range of supporting premiums

There is unit mass each of H and L households. Each earns10, consumes exactly one dwelling and has no moving cost. Neighborhood A has one fixed unit of housing; B has competitive supply at rent2 sufficient for either group. A housing is owned by price-taking landlords with opportunity rent2, and its operating costs are already included in that alternative. Utility is wage minus rent plus an amenity value: A gives H value4 and L value1; B's amenity value is zero. Let Δ=r_A−2. Values and wages are numeraire utility units, not measured social rankings of groups.

H weakly chooses A iffΔ≤4; L weakly chooses B iffΔ≥1. Thus every premium Δ∈[1,4] supports H in A and L in B, with indifferent marginal groups allocated to clear the market at the endpoints. For1<Δ<4 both group choices are strict. Any premium below1 generates excess A demand and above4 insufficient demand. Reversing the allocation cannot be supported because it would requireΔ≤1 andΔ≥4 simultaneously. The allocation is determined, but the rent level is not unique.

At the illustrative selectionΔ=2, rents are(4,2), H utility10 and L utility8. Total rent is6 and household utility sums to18, including the amenity. Net of the two homes' common opportunity service cost4, total surplus is20. The amenity raises combined household/owner surplus by4 relative to both groups using B-quality housing with the same real opportunity costs. The markers are (wage,Brent,Hvalue,Lvalue,selected premium)=(10,2,4,1,2) and (premium lower,premium upper,Arent,Hutility,Lutility,rent receipts,total net surplus)=(1,4,4,10,8,6,20). The4rent payment to A's owner is not itself an additional resource benefit.

Suppose an amenity improvement adds1to both groups' A values, costs1/2real good, and is funded by a lump-sum charge1/2to the A owner. The supporting premium interval shifts to[2,5]. If the selected premium moves from2to3, the assignment and both household utilities stay unchanged: the direct benefit is capitalized into A rent. The A owner receives one extra rent and pays1/2, gaining1/2net; aggregate net benefit is also1/2. This is a supported incidence comparison, not a theorem that every equilibrium selection or every real park leaves renters unaffected. Under the nonunique price correspondence, incidence requires an explicit selection or adjustment assumption.

4. Distribution depends on people, prices and aggregation

Inequality can mean dispersion of income, wealth, consumption or opportunity. Specify whether the measure is before or after taxes, before or after housing costs, and adjusted for household size or local prices. An identical cash income may purchase different housing bundles in different places; a homeowner's capital gain differs from a renter's higher recurring bill. Distributional analysis should state whose ownership and which date are included.

For n equally weighted nonnegative incomes y with positive sum, the Gini coefficient is G=ΣᵢΣⱼ|yᵢ−yⱼ|/(2nΣᵢyᵢ). Equivalently sum each unordered pair once and divide by nΣy. It is scale invariant because multiplying every income by a positive constant multiplies numerator and denominator equally. It is not a poverty measure or a causal decomposition. Replacing each person's income with a neighborhood mean discards within-area information; different spatial arrangements can leave the national income vector unchanged.

Worked case 4 — less inequality between neighborhoods, unchanged inequality among people

Four people earn (2,4,8,10), total24. Unordered absolute gaps sum2+6+8+4+6+2=28. Thus G=28/(4·24)=7/24. Initially A houses incomes(2,4)and B houses(8,10). Replacing incomes with their neighborhood means gives(3,3,9,9), G=1/4. Within-neighborhood pair gaps contribute4/96=1/24to the original G, and cross-neighborhood gaps24/96=1/4; these particular contributions add to7/24.

Reassign households so A has(2,10)and B has(4,8), without changing anyone's income. Both neighborhood means are6, so the mean-replaced G is zero. Actual personal G remains7/24. Within-area pair gaps now sum12and cross-area gaps16, contributing1/8and1/6. The cross-pair term is positive despite equal neighborhood means, because the distributions overlap. The comparison is (personal,initial means,reshuffled means,initial within,initial cross,reshuffled within,reshuffled cross)=(7/24,1/4,0,1/24,1/4,1/8,1/6). A general decomposition into within and between mean inequality alone needs additional terms or a different decomposable measure; a convenient special ordering must not be assumed universally.

A real transfer of2from the person earning10to the person earning2instead changes incomes to(4,4,8,8), keeping total24but lowering G to1/6. All rankings are maintained weakly; the gap sum falls from28to16. This is a genuine change in the distribution of disposable income. Whether it is socially desirable also depends on the stipulated welfare criterion, delivery costs and behavioral responses. By contrast, multiplying every original income by2keeps G at7/24while raising each person's cash resources. Neither a spatial reshuffle nor a scale-invariant statistic alone summarizes changes in living standards.

5. Neighborhood effects and the people induced to move

A correlation between residence and outcomes mixes place effects with selection. Families may choose locations using unobserved resources, information or expected opportunities; employers and services also locate endogenously. The Chetty–Hendren–Katz author manuscript studies random voucher offers and later outcomes. Its discussion explicitly distinguishes effects for different ages from conclusively identifying a pure exposure-duration mechanism, since age at move, disruption and exposure length are linked. This chapter uses that design distinction, not its numerical estimates or a claim that a new voucher scheme will have the same effect.

Define assignment Z, a specified moving treatment D and potential outcomes Y(d). Under random assignment, no defiers, a nonzero first stage and exclusion of direct assignment effects, the difference in mean outcomes divided by the difference in moving rates identifies the average effect for compliers. That group consists of families who move under the offer but would not without it. A treatment that bundles counseling, subsidies and eligibility rules cannot automatically be reduced to a scalar neighborhood-quality index: the exclusion and treatment definition must support that interpretation.

Worked case 5 — an offer effect, a complier effect and a population effect

In a synthetic population, proportions are2/5compliers,1/5always-movers and2/5never-movers. Their untreated outcomes are20,30and10; moving gains are6,4and2respectively. Each family has identical outcomes within its type, and assignment is an independent fair coin. Outcomes are an illustrative long-run index, not actual earnings or welfare. Compliers move exactly when offered, always-movers under either assignment, and never-movers under neither. No other assignment effect or interference occurs. Inputs are (complier share,always share,never share,Y0c,Y0a,Y0n,gainc,gaina,gainn)=(2/5,1/5,2/5,20,30,10,6,4,2).

Control mean is(2/5)20+(1/5)34+(2/5)10=94/5. Offer mean is(2/5)26+(1/5)34+(2/5)10=106/5. Moving rates are1/5and3/5. Thus ITT=12/5, first stage2/5and Wald effect6. The population ATE is(2/5)6+(1/5)4+(2/5)2=4, a different object. The checked vector is (control,offer,ITT,firststage,LATE,ATE)=(94/5,106/5,12/5,2/5,6,4). The population ATE is known only because this teaching model gives all types' potential outcomes; the randomized offer data alone would not reveal it.

Pooling both assignments, movers have mass2/5and outcome total(1/5)26+(1/5)34=12, mean30. Nonmovers have mass3/5and outcome total(1/5)20+(2/5)10=8, mean40/3. The raw mover difference50/3is far above6. Randomizing offers does not randomize the final mover population. Report the assignment effect for its original target and the complier interpretation only under its additional assumptions.

Mechanism identification needs another step. Suppose two age-specific causal moving effects are8at age8and2at age14, measured at age18. The model gain=θ(18−age)−d fits both withθ=1,d=2. But a model withθ=0and age-specific direct moving benefits8and2fits equally well. These observations alone do not identify a constant disruption cost versus an exposure mechanism. Multiple horizons, defensible restrictions or additional variation are needed. Evidence of heterogeneous effects is already useful; it need not be overstated as proof of one channel.

An urban policy comparison that follows people and payments

Fix the geographic unit and map commuting, housing and service links beyond its border. Track original residents even when they leave, and separately report outcomes for current residents. Distinguish rents, asset prices, physical quality, ownership and real building costs. An apparent price increase may combine a better dwelling with a scarcer location. A tax-funded amenity should include its operating and capital costs, not only construction.

Estimate or bound the margins that drive the decision: housing response, migration costs, workplace access, household preferences, displacement and local externalities. State the horizon on which each can adjust. A pilot serving a few families can leave rents unchanged while a large program bids up a fixed stock; transport then requires an equilibrium model or evidence at the relevant scale. Prespecify a comparison and a way to detect spillovers rather than treating a neighboring area as unaffected by default.

Report both resources and distribution. A landlord gain, a renter loss and a construction bill are different entries; include each payer and recipient once. Distributional weights or rights-based constraints may change the preferred policy even when total surplus rises. Evidence can discipline the consequences without deciding those values. The next chapter combines this discipline with administrative and political feasibility to build a policy recommendation that can actually be implemented and evaluated.

Exercises

  1. In the closed linear city keep N=4,w=20,r_A=1but let t=3/2. Derive the rent schedule, common utility, total commuting, rent and net resources after agricultural opportunity cost. Compare with the t=2baseline.
  2. In the open-city variant retain outside utility11,wage20and agricultural rent1. Set t=4/3. Compute population, total rent and differential rent. Explain why this does not identify national welfare without the origin economy.
  3. Solve the uncapped two-city economy when A wage is22. Give populations, rents, common utility, aggregate worker consumption, owner surplus and total surplus. Verify its global resource optimum.
  4. For the original wages20and16, impose A cap k=5. Compute rents, utility, total owner surplus and total surplus. Derive the gain from increasing the cap to6and compare it with the marginal value at5. Why can a one-unit discrete gain differ from the initial derivative?
  5. In the sorting model change H's A value to6, retaining L's value1. Find the full supporting premium interval and each group's utility atΔ=3. Does observing premium3reveal that the average willingness to pay equals3? Prove the answer from the inequalities.
  6. Under the original amenity improvement, use the supported premium adjustment2to3and owner levy1/2. Reconcile household, owner and aggregate changes. Then show that unchangedΔ=2also supports the improved allocation, and compute incidence under that different selection. State what remains invariant.
  7. Calculate the Gini for(4,4,8,8)and for twice the original vector. Prove scale invariance from the pairwise formula. Explain why zero Gini of neighborhood means need not imply equal personal incomes.
  8. Keep the mobility population but suppose the offer directly adds1to the outcome of every family, beyond any effect of moving. Derive the offer mean, ITT and naive Wald ratio. Identify exactly which assumption fails and whether the complier moving effect changed.
  9. Using the original mobility model, prove the pooled mover/nonmover means from type-assignment probabilities. Then solve the two-age constant-disruption equations and construct the alternative zero-exposure model. Distinguish the identified assignment effect from an unidentified mechanism.
  10. Design an evaluation of a housing-supply expansion bundled with transport access. State why higher local average income is insufficient evidence of better opportunities for original low-income residents.

It records property ownership, rents net of quality, sales prices, housing units and real building/operating costs, transit use and time, fiscal finance and compensation actually paid. A credible counterfactual might use a prespecified phased rollout with comparable eligible places, but assignment and anticipation must be defended; adjacent areas can receive displaced demand or accessibility gains. Estimate short-run fixed-stock effects separately from construction and migration responses. An original-resident income increase can be offset by housing costs or displacement; a higher current-resident average can arise entirely from composition. Rival mechanisms include productivity/access improvements and sorting of richer households. A prespecified trigger could halt the next phase if original low-income residents' real disposable resources fall beyond a justified tolerance despite rising property values, pending redesign of supply or compensation. Full credit requires all requested populations/accounts/horizons, a credible comparison and falsifiable revision rule, without treating the numerical toy models as measured policy elasticities.

Teach-back

Explain why rent can fall after better transport in a closed city but differential land rent can rise when the same improvement attracts newcomers. Then explain why lower inequality of neighborhood means need not reduce personal inequality.

Answer guide

With fixed population and fixed lots, lower commuting costs flatten the rent gradient and raise worker utility at the unchanged boundary. With outside utility pinned, entry expands the boundary and the rent base. These are different equilibrium closures. Replacing individual incomes by area means discards within-area dispersion; moving the same people between areas can equalize means without changing any income.

Delayed retention

After a week, derive the rent gradient from equal utility; solve a housing-cap migration equilibrium; give the full premium interval supporting two-type sorting; compute a four-person Gini; and state why random voucher offers do not make mover/nonmover comparisons random.

Retention key

Equal w−r−txand boundary opportunity rent give r(x)=r_A+t(N−x). Under the two-city cap, B housing determines common utility and A's scarcity rent adjusts to clear its limited stock. Sorting requires the premium lie between low and high amenity values, including clearing ties. Sum unordered absolute income gaps and divide by nΣy. Final moves depend on compliance type, so the pooled mover contrast selects different baseline outcomes even under randomized offers.

Scope and extension

The sources provide bounded land/housing and experimental-design context; every numerical allocation, resource account and inequality calculation is original. Extensions include endogenous density, multiple employment centers, borrowing constraints, agglomeration and congestion, discrimination and search, heterogeneous housing demand and migration costs. Those mechanisms require additional assumptions and evidence. Policy synthesis and institutional feasibility next brings these distinctions into an integrated decision process.
